overview: Pskov was a northwestern Rus city with its own civic institutions, law and coinage. Its builders developed a distinctive church architecture beside the Velikaya River. Moscow ended its republican government in 1510, although local crafts, buildings and urban life continued.

periods.title: Merchants before full independence
periods.summary: Birchbark letters preserve thirteenth-century business between named townspeople.

periods.title: The independent republic
periods.summary: Pskov enjoyed independent government from 1348 and developed its own judicial charter.

periods.title: Under Moscow
periods.summary: Vasily III abolished the republic’s assembly and installed Muscovite government.

items.text: Pskov’s builders combined compact, roughly cubic church bodies with domes, porches and open belfries. Their use of local building materials and restrained decoration gave the city a recognizable architectural character. The school reached particular prominence in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries.

Churches stood within gardens, walls and fences rather than appearing as isolated monuments. UNESCO recognizes ten surviving religious monuments representing this architectural tradition. The whole group spans several centuries, so its oldest and newest buildings should not all be imagined standing together in republican Pskov.

The veche, or civic assembly, was an important institution of Pskov’s republic. Its bell could call people together and became a powerful symbol of local government. In January 1510, Vasily III ordered the bell removed and the assembly and elected posadnik offices abolished.

Pskov began issuing its own coins in 1425, including the denga and a smaller denomination called the chetverettsa. Different principalities still used their own monetary systems. A merchant therefore needed to recognize more than a coin’s shine before agreeing that a payment was sufficient.

Some Pskov coins show Prince Dovmont holding a sword, while others carry a leopard on the reverse. The museum dates the leopard design from 1460. These images made civic identity portable: a little piece of Pskov could travel in somebody’s money pouch.

The Judicial Charter survives in manuscript copies made after the republic’s ending. Its text combines several layers of law, and scholars debate its compilation dates. Modern editors divide it into 120 articles covering courts, property, inheritance and offences, a remarkably detailed window into the disputes people expected to face.

The charter allowed a master craftsman to sue for unpaid wages. It also recognized certain property claims by dependent workers and herdsmen. Making something useful and actually getting paid could be separate problems, familiar enough to need written rules.

Women could inherit property and make wills. If a husband died without a will, his widow could use his property while she remained unmarried. These rules tell us how lawmakers organized household security; they do not establish that every widow could easily enforce her rights.

The charter required children to support their parents or risk losing their inheritance. Family care thus appeared in property law as well as personal obligation. It is a practical reminder that medieval households had to plan for ageing relatives, just as they had to plan for children.

An earlier birchbark letter from Kiurik and Gerasim asks Onfim to send squirrel skins because customers want them. It also complains that a man named Ksinofont has damaged their business. The catalogue places the letter around 1260 to 1280: medieval commerce came with impatient messages and troublesome partners.

Another letter asks Vatsiuta to load cloth promptly onto a boat and present it as his own. The sender promises to settle the transport charge. This late thirteenth- or early fourteenth-century message makes river transport tangible, down to the awkward question of who would pay for the journey.

Pskov letter 6 begins “ѿ кюрика и ѿ герасима”, meaning “From Kiurik and from Gerasim”. These are historical Cyrillic forms in the scholarly transcription, with word divisions added by editors. The greeting introduces an ordinary commercial letter, rather than a royal proclamation or a church service.

ending.text: Vasily III of Moscow ended Pskov’s republican institutions in 1510 and replaced their authority with his governors. Pskov remained an inhabited and productive city. The map’s 1530 endpoint is an imported coverage boundary, not the republic’s ending date.
